plan.question: What do recruiters actually look for in the first few seconds they spend skimming a resume?
plan.why: Everything else on the resume should be organized around surviving that initial scan, so this is the highest-leverage facet.

plan.question: How do I write a professional summary that hooks the reader and doesn't sound like a generic filler paragraph?
plan.why: The summary is often the first section read, so it needs to quickly communicate who you are and why you're a fit.

plan.question: How can I show measurable results and metrics for the work I've done, even if I don't have obvious numbers?
plan.why: Hiring managers trust concrete outcomes over vague descriptions, so quantifying impact is a core differentiator.

plan.question: How do I phrase bullet points so they sound like real engineering achievements instead of a list of job duties?
plan.why: The experience section lives or dies by bullet points, and the wording determines whether your contributions feel significant.

plan.question: How do I make sure my resume gets through an applicant tracking system and doesn't get filtered out before a human sees it?
plan.why: Many applications are screened by software first, so keyword placement and formatting compatibility are essential.

plan.question: How much should I customize my resume for a specific job description, and exactly what parts should change?
plan.why: A one-size-fits-all resume misses the signals a particular role is asking for, while targeted tailoring dramatically improves fit.

plan.question: What layout, section order, and visual formatting make a tech resume easy to read and professionally clean?
plan.why: Readability and visual hierarchy affect both the human eye and ATS parsers, so layout is a practical mechanical concern.

plan.question: How long should a software engineer or data scientist resume be, and when is it okay to go to two pages?
plan.why: Page length decisions signal judgment about relevance and experience level, and getting it wrong can hurt the first impression.

plan.question: How should I list programming languages, tools, and frameworks so a recruiter can see my stack at a glance?
plan.why: A scannable skills section helps quickly match your technical background against the role's requirements.

plan.facet: Data science and ML role differences
plan.question: If I'm targeting data science or machine learning roles, what should my resume show that a general software resume wouldn't?
plan.why: Data and AI roles value different signals, like model outcomes and domain depth, so this facet clarifies role-specific emphasis.

gaps.missing: No criterion requires the resume to include name and contact information (email, phone, LinkedIn/GitHub) or checks that they are present and professional.
gaps.why: A recruiter cannot reach an applicant without contact info; this is the first thing a skimming reviewer looks for, and none of the existing criteria mention it.
gaps.probe: What contact information should be on a resume and where should it go?

gaps.missing: No criterion requires dates for each role or checks that employment history is in reverse chronological order with no unexplained gaps.
gaps.why: Reviewers need to know recency and tenure; a resume without dates cannot be skimmed for career progression, and none of the existing page/summary/keyword rules cover this.
gaps.probe: How should employment dates and gaps be presented on a resume?

gaps.missing: No criterion checks spelling, grammar, punctuation, or typo-level polish on the actual text.
gaps.why: Typos and grammar errors are an immediate red flag for recruiters, and even a well-keyworded, quantified resume fails if it looks careless; none of the criteria evaluate language quality.
gaps.probe: How do typos and grammar mistakes affect a resume and what should you proofread?

gaps.missing: No criterion requires or checks for a projects/portfolio section or links to code, GitHub, or a personal site for technical roles.
gaps.why: For software engineers and data scientists, evidence of real projects is often as important as work history, but the pack only mentions Projects in passing and gives no way to judge whether such evidence exists.
gaps.probe: Should a software engineer or data scientist include projects, GitHub links, or a portfolio on their resume?

kept.criterion: Keep the resume to one page.
kept.check: Count the pages in the submitted PDF or printout; fail if it exceeds one page.

kept.criterion: Include only content that is relevant to the target role, with no hobbies, OS basics, or other fluff.
kept.check: Scan for banned categories—hobbies, obvious software literacy like Mac OS or Windows, and unrelated education—and fail if any such item appears on the resume.

kept.criterion: Write every experience bullet as a full sentence that states what you did, how you did it, and the result.
kept.check: For each bullet under Experience, identify an action verb, a method or context, and an outcome; fail any bullet that is a generic duty with no result, such as "handled various operational duties over five years."

kept.criterion: Rewrite the professional summary for each application so it names the specific role, stack, and experience the job posting asks for.
kept.check: Compare the summary to the target job description; flag it if it is generic boilerplate, contains no skill or technology from the posting, or is longer than one to two sentences.

kept.criterion: Back up every claim in the summary and experience bullets with a concrete fact: a number, a percentage, a dollar amount, or a specific accomplishment from a previous role.
kept.check: Highlight all claims of skill, experience, or quality; for each, require an adjacent numeral or a reference to a specific previous result; flag any statement that only describes responsibilities or enthusiasm.

kept.criterion: Quantify every outcome you claim with a concrete number.
kept.check: Read each experience bullet and the professional summary; any bullet that claims an outcome—improved performance, reduced cost, built a system—must contain a numeral (score, percentage, count, or amount).

kept.criterion: Match the resume to the job description by reflecting its repeated keywords.
kept.check: Use the find shortcut to count keywords in the job description, group them into soft skills, technical skills, and product qualities, then look for corresponding terms in the resume; a keyword that appears repeatedly in the job description but has no match in the resume fails.

kept.criterion: For each experience bullet, state the method, reason, and result, not just the task.
kept.check: Flag any bullet that names only a deliverable or duty (built dashboards, worked on X) and tells the reader nothing about how it was done, why it was done, or what it produced.

kept.criterion: Tailor the resume to the job description so the target role title and its hard-skill keywords appear in the top sections and skills list.
kept.check: Compare the resume against the job description; fail if the exact or near-exact target job title is missing from the header or summary, or if any required hard skill from the job description is absent from the skills section.

kept.criterion: Write every experience bullet as an action-oriented accomplishment with a concrete result, not a generic responsibility.
kept.check: For each role, flag any bullet that describes a duty without an action verb and a measurable outcome; fail the resume if a single responsibility-only bullet appears in the experience section.

kept.criterion: Open with a professional summary that names the target role, states your experience level, and brags about a specific accomplishment by the second sentence.
kept.check: Read the first section; fail if it is only an objective statement, if the role title is not matched, if experience years/environments are absent, or if the first two sentences contain no concrete accomplishment.

kept.criterion: Use the same keywords from the job description in your resume so the ATS matches it to the role.
kept.check: Compare the target job description's required skills/tools against the resume; pass only if every required keyword from the posting appears somewhere in the resume.

kept.criterion: Give the last 5-7 years of experience the most space; compress older roles to at most two or three relevant bullet points.
kept.check: For every role that ended more than seven years ago, count the bullet points; fail if any such role has more than three bullet points or is given as much space as recent experience.

kept.criterion: Format the resume for ATS parsing: use a single column, no tables/images/graphics, and a basic font like Ariel or Times New Roman.
kept.check: Reject if the resume has a multi-column layout, a table, an image, a graphic, a text box, or a decorative font; accept only simple left-to-right text in a standard font.

kept.criterion: Tailor the resume to the target job description by including its required skills, keywords, and tech stack in the skills and experience sections.
kept.check: Compare the job description's required technologies and repeated keywords against the resume; if any required skill is absent or represented only by a different stack, fail.

kept.criterion: Write each experience bullet as a quantified accomplishment, not a list of duties.
kept.check: For every bullet under Experience and Projects, verify that it names a concrete result with a number or an explicit outcome; bullets that only describe responsibilities fail.

added.check: Open the submitted file and look for embedded images, skill bars, sparklines, two-column layouts, and custom template graphics; fail if any are present.

added.criterion: Mirror the job description's required keywords and tech stack in the resume before submitting it.
added.check: Place the target job description next to the resume and compare required skills and tools; fail the resume if a core requirement is absent or the resume leads with a different stack than the posting.

added.check: Compare the skills section to the job description and to the rest of the resume; fail if it contains generic or unrelated skills, or if any listed skill never appears in a work or project bullet.

refused.criterion: Tailor the resume to each job posting by mirroring its wording and including the required tech stack, instead of sending one generic resume.
Remove sections and decorations that don't help a hiring decision: objective statements, hobbies, references, photos, skill-rating bars, and Udemy-style certificates.
Use a single-column, ATS-friendly layout: no custom templates with images, charts, tables, columns, headers, footers, emojis, symbols, colors, or highlights.

kept.criterion: Keep the resume to one page.
kept.check: Count the pages in the submitted PDF or printout; fail if it exceeds one page.

kept.criterion: Include only content that is relevant to the target role, with no hobbies, OS basics, or other fluff.
kept.check: Scan for banned categories—hobbies, obvious software literacy like Mac OS or Windows, and unrelated education—and fail if any such item appears on the resume.

kept.criterion: Write every experience bullet as a full sentence that states what you did, how you did it, and the result.
kept.check: For each bullet under Experience, identify an action verb, a method or context, and an outcome; fail any bullet that is a generic duty with no result, such as "handled various operational duties over five years."

kept.criterion: Rewrite the professional summary for each application so it names the specific role, stack, and experience the job posting asks for.
kept.check: Compare the summary to the target job description; flag it if it is generic boilerplate, contains no skill or technology from the posting, or is longer than one to two sentences.

kept.criterion: Back up every claim in the summary and experience bullets with a concrete fact: a number, a percentage, a dollar amount, or a specific accomplishment from a previous role.
kept.check: Highlight all claims of skill, experience, or quality; for each, require an adjacent numeral or a reference to a specific previous result; flag any statement that only describes responsibilities or enthusiasm.

kept.criterion: Quantify every outcome you claim with a concrete number.
kept.check: Read each experience bullet and the professional summary; any bullet that claims an outcome—improved performance, reduced cost, built a system—must contain a numeral (score, percentage, count, or amount).

kept.criterion: Match the resume to the job description by reflecting its repeated keywords.
kept.check: Use the find shortcut to count keywords in the job description, group them into soft skills, technical skills, and product qualities, then look for corresponding terms in the resume; a keyword that appears repeatedly in the job description but has no match in the resume fails.

kept.criterion: For each experience bullet, state the method, reason, and result, not just the task.
kept.check: Flag any bullet that names only a deliverable or duty (built dashboards, worked on X) and tells the reader nothing about how it was done, why it was done, or what it produced.

kept.criterion: Tailor the resume to the job description so the target role title and its hard-skill keywords appear in the top sections and skills list.
kept.check: Compare the resume against the job description; fail if the exact or near-exact target job title is missing from the header or summary, or if any required hard skill from the job description is absent from the skills section.

kept.criterion: Write every experience bullet as an action-oriented accomplishment with a concrete result, not a generic responsibility.
kept.check: For each role, flag any bullet that describes a duty without an action verb and a measurable outcome; fail the resume if a single responsibility-only bullet appears in the experience section.

kept.criterion: Open with a professional summary that names the target role, states your experience level, and brags about a specific accomplishment by the second sentence.
kept.check: Read the first section; fail if it is only an objective statement, if the role title is not matched, if experience years/environments are absent, or if the first two sentences contain no concrete accomplishment.

kept.criterion: Use the same keywords from the job description in your resume so the ATS matches it to the role.
kept.check: Compare the target job description's required skills/tools against the resume; pass only if every required keyword from the posting appears somewhere in the resume.

kept.criterion: Give the last 5-7 years of experience the most space; compress older roles to at most two or three relevant bullet points.
kept.check: For every role that ended more than seven years ago, count the bullet points; fail if any such role has more than three bullet points or is given as much space as recent experience.

kept.criterion: Format the resume for ATS parsing: use a single column, no tables/images/graphics, and a basic font like Ariel or Times New Roman.
kept.check: Reject if the resume has a multi-column layout, a table, an image, a graphic, a text box, or a decorative font; accept only simple left-to-right text in a standard font.

kept.criterion: Tailor the resume to the target job description by including its required skills, keywords, and tech stack in the skills and experience sections.
kept.check: Compare the job description's required technologies and repeated keywords against the resume; if any required skill is absent or represented only by a different stack, fail.

kept.criterion: Write each experience bullet as a quantified accomplishment, not a list of duties.
kept.check: For every bullet under Experience and Projects, verify that it names a concrete result with a number or an explicit outcome; bullets that only describe responsibilities fail.

added.criterion: Use a professional summary section instead of an objective statement.
added.check: Scan the top of the resume for a 'Professional Summary' or 'Summary' heading and confirm there is no 'Objective' or 'Objective Statement' heading anywhere on the page.

added.criterion: Put your location as city and state only, never a street address, and keep any LinkedIn or GitHub hyperlinks short and clean.
added.check: Find the location in the header and fail if a street address appears. Check that LinkedIn/GitHub links display as concise link text and do not run as long raw URLs across the layout.

added.criterion: Order all work and education entries in reverse chronological order and date each job with months, not just years.
added.check: Verify the most recent role is listed first, then older roles follow; confirm degrees and certifications run from most recent to oldest. Reject any job date written only as a year or a year range without months.

added.criterion: Quantify the impact in every experience bullet with a concrete number — a percentage, count, currency figure, or time reduction — rather than just listing the duty.
added.check: Read each experience bullet. If a bullet contains no numeric metric and only states a responsibility or technology used, mark it as a violation.

added.criterion: Write every experience or project bullet as an impact statement — an outcome that made or saved money, saved time, or increased productivity — rather than a list of duties or technologies.
added.check: Read each bullet in the Experience and Projects sections. Flag any bullet that only describes a task, tool, or responsibility and does not name a result or metric (money, time, productivity, performance target, user count).

added.criterion: Date every role with both month and year, and add a one-line explanation for any short stint or gap.
added.check: Check each position's date line for a month plus year (for example 'March 2022 to May 2022'). For any role lasting less than 3 months or any career break, look for a brief reason in the work experience or summary.

added.criterion: Lead with a complete contact block: full name, email, phone number, and at least city/state; if you are relocating, state the target location and date.
added.check: Look at the top of the resume for the required contact items. Fail if city/state is missing. If the resume signals relocation or out-of-state remote work, require an explicit target location and date such as 'Moving to X by Y date'; otherwise fail.

added.criterion: Write every experience/project bullet as an impact statement, not a duty list: start with a strong action verb, name the business result, and include numbers wherever possible.
added.check: For each bullet under experience/projects, confirm it begins with a concrete verb and states an outcome such as money saved, revenue made, time saved, productivity gained, or customers served. Fail bullets that only restate responsibilities or technologies. Then count bullets in each role that contain a number or percentage: fail the role if none do.
